topic.title: Estimating mean and standard deviation from grouped data
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. A grouped table is a standard opening question: Summer 2019 Q1 gave 2 marks for the estimated mean and 3 for the estimated standard deviation; Summer 2022 Q3 added a 1-mark part for why the mean is only an estimate; Summer 2024 Q1 used the same 2 and 3 split and then tested a linear change. The command word is Calculate, with 'an estimate of' in the stem and often 'You must show your working' or an instruction to use the table. Schemes run M1 for the midpoints and fx column, W1 for the mean, MW1 for the fx squared column and M1 W1 for the substitution and the answer.
mustMemorise: The midpoint is $\dfrac{\text{lower end} + \text{upper end}}{2}$, and it stands for every item in the class
$f x^{2}$ means $f \times x^{2}$: square the midpoint first, never square the fx entry
Divide by $\sum f$, the total frequency, not by the number of classes
Both answers are estimates because the exact values inside each class are unknown
Answers to 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise
notOnThisSpec: Median, modal class and interquartile range from a grouped table, which the Teacher Guidance says will not be asked
Histograms, frequency density and cumulative frequency curves, which belong to GCSE Mathematics
The sample standard deviation with divisor $\sum f - 1$
Unequal class widths treated by any special rule: the midpoint is used whatever the width

Build the $fx$ column and total it

workedExamples.stem:
A grower measured the heights, to the nearest centimetre, of 50 tomato plants.
Calculate an estimate of the mean plant height, and an estimate of the standard deviation of those heights.

data.caption: Heights of 50 tomato plants, with the midpoint, fx and f x² columns worked out

steps.decision: A class such as 20 to 24 gives no individual heights, so each class is represented by the value in its middle. That is why the answers are estimates.
Multiply each frequency by its own midpoint and add down the column. The total frequency is what you divide by, not the number of classes.
That is the estimated mean. Keep it exactly as it is; rounding it now would shift the standard deviation.
Each entry is the frequency times the square of the midpoint. It is not the fx entry squared, and that difference is the most reported error on this question.

options: $f x^{2}$ for the third class is $18 \times 32^{2} = 18432$
$f x^{2}$ for the third class is $576^{2} = 331776$
$f x^{2}$ for the third class is $\left(18 \times 32\right) \times 2 = 1152$
whyMenu.explain: The square sits on the $x$ only, so square the midpoint and then multiply by the frequency. Squaring the fx entry gives 331776, which is far too large.

steps.decision: Substitute into the sheet's formula and finish with the square root. Two decimal places, as the front page of the paper asks.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: An estimated mean of $31.7$ cm and an estimated standard deviation of $5.69$ cm

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on something you already know. What is the midpoint of the class 7 to 9?
items.skill: Midpoint of a class (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: That is the bottom end of the class. The midpoint is the value halfway along it.
That is the top of the class. Add the two ends and halve them.

items.stem: Before the lesson: in a frequency table, what does the frequency column tell you?
items.skill: Reading a frequency table (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.text: How many items fall in that class
options.feedback: Yes, and adding that column gives the total number of items, which is what you divide by.

options.text: The size of the items in that class
options.feedback: Size is in the class column. The frequency counts how many items are there.
Width comes from the two ends of the class. Frequency is a count.

items.stem: Before the lesson, and you are not meant to know this yet: a table gives classes rather than individual measurements. What is lost?
items.skill: Why grouped answers are estimates (new here, so a guess is fine)

options.text: The individual values, so every answer becomes an estimate
options.feedback: Exactly the reason examiners want in words, and the reason the midpoint is used at all.

options.text: Nothing: the class tells you each value
options.feedback: A class of 20 to 24 could hold any of those heights. That is what makes the answer an estimate.
The total survives: it is the frequency column added up. What is lost is the individual values.

items.stem: A class has frequency $18$ and midpoint $32$. What is its $f x^{2}$ entry?
items.skill: Building the f x squared column

options.feedback: Yes: $18 \times 32^{2} = 18432$. Square the midpoint, then multiply.
That is the fx entry squared, $\left(576\right)^{2}$. The square belongs on the midpoint alone.
That is the fx entry with no squaring at all. The second column needs the midpoint squared first.

items.stem: A grouped table has 5 classes and $\sum f = 50$. What do you divide $\sum fx$ by?
items.skill: Dividing by the total frequency, not the number of classes

options.feedback: Yes. The mean shares the total out over every item, and there are that many items.
That is the number of classes. Examiners name this as the one major method error on this question.
That is the fx total itself, which is the number you are dividing, not the divisor.

items.stem: Which sentence earns the mark for why a grouped mean is only an estimate?

options.text: The exact values in each class are unknown, so the midpoint stands for them all
options.feedback: Yes. It names what is missing and what replaced it, which is the whole mark.

options.text: Because the numbers have been rounded
options.feedback: Rounding is a different idea, and the mark is not there. Say that the individual values are unknown.

options.text: Because a mean is always approximate
options.feedback: A mean of raw values is exact. It is the grouping that makes this one an estimate.

items.stem: For a grouped set, $\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} = 1037.3$ and $\bar{x} = 31.7$. What is the estimated standard deviation?
items.skill: Subtracting the mean squared, then rooting

options.feedback: That is the variance, the number under the root. One more step finishes it.
The mean squared was never taken off, so that is roughly the size of a plant rather than the spread of the heights.

items.stem: In a table of continuous data the class is 5 to under 10 minutes. Which value goes in the $x$ column?

options.feedback: Yes: halfway between 5 and 10.
That is the lower end. Using it drags every estimate down.
That is the upper end, and a time of exactly that would belong to the next class. Take the value halfway along instead.

parts.stem:
A grouped table gives the heights of 50 tomato plants in classes such as 20 to 24 centimetres.
Explain why the mean height calculated from the table is only an estimate.

accepted: The exact values inside each class are not known, so the midpoint is used to stand for every value in the class.
The table only gives classes, so the exact values are not known and midpoints are used instead.

scheme.for: the exact heights inside each class are unknown, so each class is represented by its midpoint

hints: What does the table not tell you?
Say what is used in place of the real values.
parts.workedSolution: The table records only which class each plant falls in. The exact heights are not known, so every plant in a class is treated as having the midpoint height, and the mean that follows is an estimate.

commonErrors.feedback: Rounding is not the reason. The reason is that the table never records the individual heights, so each class is represented by its midpoint. Say that, and the mark is there.
Sample size is a different idea. The word 'estimate' is there because the exact values inside each class are unknown and the midpoint stands in for them.

questions.solutionProgram: no computation: the mark is for naming the unknown individual values and the midpoint that replaces them

findTheMistake.stem: Daniel was asked for an estimate of the standard deviation for these cone counts (10 to 12, 13 to 15, 16 to 18, 19 to 21, 22 to 24 with frequencies 6, 8, 14, 8, 4). His working:
studentWorking: sd = square root of (107608 over 40 minus 16.7 squared) = 49.11
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 squares each entry of the fx column. The column the formula needs is $f \times x^{2}$: square the midpoint and then multiply by the frequency, which gives 726, 1568, 4046, 3200, 2116.
correction: f x squared column is 726, 1568, 4046, 3200, 2116, total 11656

findTheMistake.feedback: The midpoints and the mean are right, so the first method-and-working mark is safe. The mark for $\sum fx^{2}$ is lost at line 3, and the answer inherits it. prompts.prompt: The five columns of a grouped mean and standard deviation table.
prompts.answer: Class, frequency $f$, midpoint $x$, $fx$, and $f x^{2}$. Total the $f$, $fx$ and $f x^{2}$ columns.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between $f x^{2}$ and $\left(fx\right)^{2}$?
prompts.answer: $f x^{2}$ squares the midpoint and then multiplies by the frequency. $\left(fx\right)^{2}$ squares the whole fx entry, which is much larger and is not what the formula wants.

prompts.prompt: Why is a mean calculated from a grouped table only an estimate?
prompts.answer: The table records only which class each item falls in, so the exact values are unknown and every item in a class is treated as sitting at the midpoint.

prompts.prompt: The estimated standard deviation of a grouped distribution, as the sheet prints it.
prompts.answer: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} - \bar{x}^{2}}$, with $x$ the class midpoints.

prompts.prompt: You have $\sum fx$. What do you divide it by, and what must you not divide it by?
prompts.answer: Divide by $\sum f$, the total frequency. Do not divide by the number of classes.
